posts.claim: Ulama—especially ulama de cadera in Sinaloa—is a living, endangered descendant/tradition of the pre-Hispanic Mesoamerican ballgame. The wider ballgame tradition has archaeological evidence reaching at least the second millennium BCE (including a formal court dated about 1650 BCE), so describing the tradition as roughly 3,400–3,500 years old is reasonable; that dating should not be presented as proof that today’s ulama has remained unchanged for that entire period.

posts.central_knowledge_unit: Major Taylor | Cycling, Racism, Records, Nickname, & Biography | Britannica
posts.claim: Marshall Walter “Major” Taylor was an Indianapolis-born Black American professional cyclist who won the mile sprint at the 1899 Montréal world championships; the UCI’s historical palmarès lists M. Taylor (USA) as the 1899 Montréal sprint winner. Archival and institutional accounts document his national and international racing prominence, racial exclusion and hostility during his career, and his 1928 autobiography, The Fastest Bicycle Rider in the World. The National Museum of American History characterizes him as the first African American world champion in any sport. The exact day of his birth should not be stated as settled: Britannica gives November 27, 1878, while the University of Pittsburgh archive, Library of Congress authority record, and 2023 congressional bill text give November 26, 1878.
